prompt: I forgot to take my morning tablet. What should I do?
completion: It depends on the medicine, so check the leaflet or ask your pharmacist. As a general rule, do not take two doses together to make up for a missed one. Mark the dose as missed in your record so your family and doctor can see it.

prompt: Can I take a double dose if I missed one yesterday?
completion: No. Taking a double dose can be harmful with many medicines. Take your next dose at the usual time and ask your pharmacist or doctor if you are unsure what to do about the missed one.

prompt: What does 'take after food' mean?
completion: It means take the medicine during a meal or within about half an hour after eating. Food helps protect the stomach and helps some medicines work properly.

prompt: What does 'take on an empty stomach' mean?
completion: It usually means at least one hour before food or two hours after food. Some medicines are absorbed poorly when taken with a meal. Your pharmacist can confirm the timing for your medicine.

prompt: Why do I have to take some tablets at the same time every day?
completion: Taking a medicine at the same time keeps a steady amount of it in your body, so it works evenly through the day. A fixed time also makes it easier to remember.

prompt: Is it safe to crush my tablets because they are hard to swallow?
completion: Do not crush or split a tablet unless your pharmacist says it is safe. Some tablets are made to release slowly, and crushing them can release too much at once. Ask your pharmacist about a liquid or smaller form.

prompt: Can I stop my blood pressure tablets now that my readings are normal?
completion: Do not stop on your own. Normal readings often mean the medicine is working. Talk to your doctor, who can decide whether the dose should change.

prompt: I feel dizzy after taking my medicine. What should I do?
completion: Sit or lie down until the dizziness passes, and get up slowly. Tell your doctor or pharmacist soon, because the dose or timing may need adjusting. If you faint, fall, or have chest pain, get emergency help.

prompt: How should I store my medicines?
completion: Keep them in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight, and out of reach of children. A bathroom is often too damp. Some medicines, such as insulin, need to be kept in the fridge, so check the label.

prompt: How do I know if a medicine has expired?
completion: Look for the expiry date printed on the box, strip or bottle, often after the letters EXP. Do not use medicine past that date. Take expired medicine back to a pharmacy for safe disposal.

prompt: Can I take my medicines with tea or coffee?
completion: Plain water is best. Tea, coffee, milk and juice can change how some medicines are absorbed. If you are unsure about a particular medicine, ask your pharmacist.

prompt: Can I drink grapefruit juice with my tablets?
completion: Grapefruit juice affects several common medicines, including some for cholesterol and blood pressure. Ask your pharmacist whether it matters for yours before drinking it regularly.

prompt: What should I bring to my doctor's appointment?
completion: Bring a list of all your medicines with doses, including vitamins and herbal products. Also bring any recent test reports, a note of symptoms or missed doses, and the questions you want to ask.

prompt: How can I remember what the doctor tells me?
completion: Write your questions down before the visit and note the answers during it. You can ask the doctor to repeat or write down the main points, and it helps to bring a family member or caretaker.

prompt: What questions should I ask when I get a new medicine?
completion: Ask what it is for, how and when to take it, how long to take it, what side effects to watch for, and whether it is safe with your other medicines.

prompt: Is it all right to share my medicine with my husband who has the same problem?
completion: No. A medicine is prescribed for one person's condition, weight, age and other medicines. Sharing can be dangerous. He should see a doctor for his own prescription.

prompt: Can I take a painkiller along with my regular medicines?
completion: Some painkillers can affect blood pressure, kidneys, the stomach or blood-thinning medicine. Check with your pharmacist or doctor before taking one, even if it is sold without a prescription.

prompt: I take many medicines. How can I keep track of them?
completion: Keep one up-to-date list with the name, dose, time and purpose of each medicine. A weekly pill organiser and reminders at fixed times also help. Share the list with your family and every doctor you see.

prompt: What is a pill organiser and how do I use it?
completion: It is a box with compartments for each day, and often for morning, afternoon, evening and night. Fill it once a week, ideally with someone checking, then take the tablets from that day's compartment.

prompt: My mother refuses to take her medicine. What can I do?
completion: Ask gently why. It may be side effects, trouble swallowing, cost or not understanding the purpose. Listen first, then share the concern with her doctor. Avoid hiding medicine in food unless a doctor or pharmacist has agreed.

prompt: How can I help my father with his medicines without taking over?
completion: Ask how he would like to be helped. Let him make the decisions and do what he can himself, such as marking doses as taken. Offer reminders and help with refills, and go to appointments if he wants company.

prompt: What are common side effects I should report?
completion: Report anything new or troubling after starting a medicine, such as a rash, swelling, dizziness, stomach pain, unusual tiredness, confusion or bleeding. Your doctor or pharmacist can tell you whether it is related.

prompt: When should I call for emergency help?
completion: Call emergency services straight away for chest pain, trouble breathing, sudden weakness or drooping on one side, trouble speaking, fainting, a serious fall, or swelling of the face or throat after a medicine.

prompt: What should I do if I think I took too much medicine?
completion: Treat it as urgent. Call emergency services or go to the nearest hospital now, and take the medicine packet with you. Do not wait for symptoms to appear.

prompt: Can I take my evening tablet early if I am going out?
completion: A small change in timing is fine for many medicines but not for all. Ask your pharmacist how flexible the timing is for your tablet before changing it.

prompt: Should I keep taking antibiotics after I feel better?
completion: Follow the course your doctor prescribed. Stopping early or saving tablets for later can let the infection return. If you have side effects, speak to your doctor instead of stopping on your own.

prompt: Why do I need blood tests while taking my medicine?
completion: Some medicines need regular checks to make sure the dose is right and that organs such as the kidneys and liver are coping well. Ask your doctor how often you need them.

prompt: Do vitamins and herbal products count as medicines?
completion: Yes, tell your doctor and pharmacist about them. Some supplements and herbal products change how prescription medicines work or add to side effects.

prompt: How do I use eye drops correctly?
completion: Wash your hands, tilt your head back, pull the lower eyelid down gently and put one drop in the pocket. Close the eye for a minute. If you use two kinds of drops, wait about five minutes between them.

prompt: How do I check my blood sugar before taking insulin?
completion: Follow the method your doctor or nurse showed you, and write the reading down with the time. If the reading is unusually low or high, or you feel shaky, sweaty or confused, contact your doctor or get help at once.

prompt: What are signs of low blood sugar?
completion: Shaking, sweating, hunger, a fast heartbeat, confusion or sudden tiredness can be signs. Follow the plan your doctor gave you, and get emergency help if the person is drowsy or cannot swallow.

prompt: How much water should I drink with a tablet?
completion: A full glass of water is a good habit unless your doctor has asked you to limit fluids. It helps the tablet go down and dissolve properly.

prompt: Can I take medicine that was prescribed for me last year for the same illness?
completion: It is safer to check first. The illness may be different this time, the medicine may have expired, and your other medicines may have changed. Ask your doctor or pharmacist.

prompt: What should I do before I run out of my medicine?
completion: Plan a refill when about a week's supply is left. Running out can interrupt treatment. A family member or caretaker can help with ordering and collecting it.

prompt: How do I travel with my medicines?
completion: Carry them in their original packs in your hand luggage, with a copy of the prescription and your medicine list. Take a few days extra and keep to your usual times as closely as you can.

prompt: My medicine looks different from last month. Is that normal?
completion: Different brands of the same medicine can look different. Check that the name and strength on the label match your prescription, and ask the pharmacist to confirm before you take it.

prompt: I have trouble reading the small print on labels. What can help?
completion: Ask the pharmacist for large-print labels or to write the instructions clearly. A magnifier, good lighting, or having the instructions read aloud can also help.

prompt: Is it normal to feel sleepy after my night tablet?
completion: Some medicines cause drowsiness, which is why they are given at night. If you feel very drowsy during the day, unsteady or confused, tell your doctor.

prompt: How can I avoid falls when I take medicines that make me dizzy?
completion: Get up slowly from bed or a chair, keep floors clear and well lit, wear steady footwear and use handrails. Tell your doctor about the dizziness, as the medicine may need reviewing.

prompt: What should I tell a new doctor about my medicines?
completion: Give the full list of medicines, doses and times, any allergies or bad reactions you have had, and your long-term conditions. Mention supplements and anything you buy without a prescription.

prompt: What is the difference between a generic and a brand medicine?
completion: A generic medicine has the same active ingredient and strength as the brand version and works the same way. It may look different and usually costs less.

prompt: Can alcohol affect my medicines?
completion: Yes. Alcohol can increase drowsiness, upset blood sugar, and interact with many medicines. Ask your pharmacist whether it is safe with yours.

prompt: How do I help my mother remember a doctor visit?
completion: Put the visit on a shared calendar, set a reminder the day before and on the morning, and arrange transport early. Prepare her questions and medicine list together the night before.

prompt: What should a caretaker write down each day?
completion: Note which doses were taken, skipped or missed, any new symptoms, meals and fluids if relevant, and anything unusual such as a fall or confusion. Short daily notes help the family and doctor.

prompt: How do I talk to my parent about needing more help with medicines?
completion: Choose a calm moment, say what you have noticed without blame, and ask what would make things easier. Agree on small steps together so they stay in control.

prompt: My father took his tablet but cannot remember if he did. What now?
completion: Do not give another dose just in case. Check the pill organiser or the dose record. Marking each dose as soon as it is taken prevents this doubt next time.

prompt: What should I do if I vomit soon after taking a tablet?
completion: It depends on the medicine and how long ago you took it. Do not take another dose until you have asked your pharmacist or doctor.

prompt: How often should my medicines be reviewed?
completion: Ask your doctor for a medicine review at least once a year, and whenever you start a new medicine, have a hospital stay, or notice new side effects.
